questions.q: How do I find out where to vote on Election Day?
questions.a:
Visit the Vermont Voter Portal (https://vote.vermont.gov) to view your polling place(s) for upcoming elections. Also see notes or directions from your clerk about the polling place. You'll need to log in using your personal information.

On the Vermont Voter Portal (https://vote.vermont.gov), you can also request and track an absentee ballot. You can update your voter registration record. You can find other information about your upcoming elections.

Download a list of polling places in Vermont (https://outside.vermont.gov/dept/sos/Elections_Division/voters/vermont_election_polling_places.pdf).

questions.q: What time do polling places open and close?
questions.a:
In Vermont, polls open between 5am and 10am, depending on the town. All polling places close at 7pm. See 17 V.S.A. §2561 (https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/17/051/02561).

For local polling place hours, please visit the Vermont Voter Portal (https://vote.vermont.gov).

questions.q: Am I required to show identification when I vote?
questions.a: No. In Vermont, only first-time voters who have registered by mail have to show ID in order to vote. If you registered when you renewed your driver’s license, or as part of a voter registration drive, you will not be required to show ID.

questions.q: What happens if I show up to vote and my name is not on the checklist even though I registered before the deadline?
questions.a: If for any reason your name is not on the voter registration list when you arrive at the polls, you can simply fill out a registration form and vote that day. Vermont now has same day voter registration.

questions.q: Can I ask for help when I go to vote?
questions.a: If you need help voting you are allowed to bring someone with you—or you can ask for assistance from the election officials.

questions.q: What happens if I make a mistake when I vote?
questions.a: If you make a mistake when you vote you can ask for a new ballot. They will take your first ballot and mark it “spoiled” so it won’t be counted, and they will give you a new ballot to vote.

questions.q: Will my ballot count if I only vote in a couple races?
questions.a: Yes. There is no requirement that a voter vote the whole ballot. Your vote will be counted in every race where you recorded a vote.

questions.q: Do I have to vote for the candidates on the ballot?
questions.a: No. You have the right to enter any name in the "write-in" space provided for each race on the ballot or to leave the ballot unmarked.

questions.q: Can I wear a shirt or button demonstrating my favorite candidate into the polling place?
questions.a: No. If you plan to wear candidate paraphernalia, you will have to cover it while inside the building containing the polling place. The polling place is about voting, not campaigning—once voters have entered the polling place the campaigns have ended.

questions.q: Can I bring candidate information in with me when I go to vote?
questions.a:
Yes. Although the rule is that there is no politicking or campaigning in the polling place (you will be asked to remove candidate buttons or stickers) you can bring anything you need to help you vote into the voting booth.

You should be careful not to publicly display any material inside the building containing the polling place and to take any material out with you when you are done!

questions.q: I am visually impaired. How can I vote?
questions.a: The Office of Secretary of State provides an Accessible Voting System (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/accessible-voting/) that serves voters with a wide range of disabilities, including blind and visually impaired voters and voters with physical disabilities. An election official will assist you once you arrive at your polling place.

questions.q: I reside outside of the United States, but I am a United States citizen. Can I still vote in the United States?
questions.a: Yes. You will need to complete a Voter Registration Application (https://outside.vermont.gov/dept/sos/Elections_Division/voters/vermont_voter_registration_form.pdf), along with an Early/Absentee Request Form (https://outside.vermont.gov/dept/sos/Elections_Division/voters/vermont_absentee_ballot_request.pdf).

questions.q: What is a provisional ballot?
questions.a:
Use of provisional ballots in Vermont is very rare. A person who is not on the checklist but asserts they submitted an application prior to the deadline is now provided an affidavit to swear to that fact. If they are willing to do so under the pains and penalty of perjury, they are allowed to vote.

Since it is very rare that someone is not on the checklist, does not assert they applied on time, but still demands to vote, the provisional ballot is rarely needed. It is only used if a person demanding to vote at the polling place is not on the checklist and the voter cannot affirm they registered to vote by the deadline.

questions.q: WHO IS ELIGIBLE TO VOTE ABSENTEE?
questions.a: In Vermont, all voters can apply to vote absentee.

questions.q: WILL MY BALLOT AUTOMATICALLY BE MAILED TO ME?
questions.a:
No. Ballots will be mailed to all registered Vermont voters upon request for most elections, such as the Annual Town Meeting, Presidential Primary, and Statewide Primary.

Ballots are automatically mailed out to all registered voters for General Elections only, which are held every November of even numbered years. This was a change in Vermont election law that passed in 2021.

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: You can request an absentee ballot through phone, fax, email, mail, in person or online. (https://mvp.vermont.gov/)

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE TO REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: The last day to request an absentee ballot is 1 day before the election. All requests must be submitted by the day before the election before the Town Clerk’s office closes for the day.

questions.q: DO I HAVE TO REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT EACH YEAR?
questions.a: Yes, the absentee ballot request form is good only for that calendar year. Per state law, the clerk is unable to keep an absentee list from year to year. Each year a new request must be made for any or all elections for that current calendar year.

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE FOR SUBMITTING A VOTED ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: Your voted ballot must be received by your town clerk by the close of the polls on Election Day.

questions.q: WHEN ARE ABSENTEE BALLOTS AVAILABLE TO VOTERS WHO HAVE REQUESTED THEM?
questions.a:
Absentee ballots for a presidential primary (March), a state primary (August), or general (November) elections are available 45 days prior to the election.

If your city or town is having a special election in August or November, the absentee ballots may not be ready until somewhere between 20 to 30 days prior to the election.

questions.q: HOW CAN I VOTE AN ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a:
There are several ways for you to vote an absentee ballot in Vermont:

- Vote at Home on Election Day. If you are sick or disabled a ballot can be delivered to your home on election day. You must request an absentee ballot before 5pm on the day before the election. On election day, two justices of the peace will deliver a ballot to you and then will bring the ballot back to the polling place so it can be counted.
- Vote by Mail. You can request that the town clerk mail you an early voter absentee ballot. Once voted, you can return the ballot to the clerk in the envelope included with the ballot. The clerk must receive the ballot by the close of the polls on Election Day to be counted. You can request a ballot at any time before an election and clerks will mail absentee ballots within the 45 days before the election.
- Hand Delivered Ballots. You can pick up a ballot at the town clerk's office at any time beginning 45 days before the general or primary election, and hand-deliver the voted ballot in a sealed envelope to the clerk on or before Election Day. The ballot can be returned to the clerk or delivered to the polling place by the voter or any person the voter authorizes to return the ballot for them. However, you can only pick up your own ballot from the clerk's office.

questions.q: HOW DO I RETURN MY VOTED ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: You have multiple options to return your ballot: you can mail it, deposit it in a secure drop box if offered in your area, or return your ballot in person at your local elections office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: CAN I TRACK MY MAILED ABSENTEE BALLOT?
questions.a: You can sign up to track your advance ballot (http://vote.vermont.gov/) on your Secretary of State website.

questions.q: WHAT IF I REQUESTED AN ABSENTEE BALLOT BUT WANT TO VOTE IN PERSON?
questions.a: If you requested an absentee ballot but want to vote in person, you must surrender your absentee ballots before receiving a regular ballot or sign an affidavit that you haven’t already voted. Do not mail a ballot and vote in person. For specifics, find your local county clerk contact info here (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST AN ABSENTEE BALLOT AS AN OVERSEAS OR US MILITARY VOTER?
questions.a: Overseas citizens and U.S. military personnel can find information on how to register to vote and request an absentee ballot at the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/vote/home.htm)

questions.q: WHO CAN REGISTER TO VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a:
You can register to vote in Vermont if you meet the following requirements:

- You are a US citizen
- You are a resident of Vermont t in the town where your residential address is, or be a military or overseas voter whose last US residence was in Vermont
- You are at least 18 years old (17-year-olds may pre-register and vote in an immediately preceding primary election if turning 18 before a general election)

You may register to vote at any time, including on Election Day. Registration is available:

- Online (https://vote.vermont.gov/public/dashboard)
- By mail - Download and print a blank Voter Registration Application here. (https://outside.vermont.gov/dept/sos/Elections_Division/voters/vermont_voter_registration_form.pdf)
- In person at your town or city clerk’s office during business hours or at your polling place on Election Day
- At the same time as applying for or renewing a motor vehicle driver's license or nondriver identification card

questions.q: WHO CAN VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a:
To vote in Vermont, you must:

- Be a US citizen
- Be a Vermont resident
- Be at least 18 years old
- Take the Voter's Oath (formerly called the Freeman's Oath)
- Be registered to vote

  - There is no deadline to register; you can register and vote on the same day. Voter registration applications must be submitted to the presiding officer at the polling location.

Youth Vote

A bill passed by the Vermont Legislature lowers the voting age to 16 for Brattleboro's local elections. This means that every resident of Brattleboro, VT, who will be 16 years of age or older on Election Day is eligible to register and vote in local elections. You must be 18 by Election Day to vote in state or federal elections.

questions.q: CAN I VOTE IN VERMONT IF I AM ATTENDING SCHOOL OUT OF STATE?
questions.a: Yes. Attending school outside Vermont doesn’t affect your voting residence. You don’t gain or lose residency just because you’re a student somewhere else.

questions.q: CAN I VOTE IN VERMONT IF I HAVE A FELONY CONVICTION?
questions.a: In Vermont, those with criminal records never lose the right to vote. If you are incarcerated, regardless of the offense, you are able to vote. You should register to vote in the town or city where you resided before incarceration.

questions.q: CAN I REGISTER AND VOTE IN VERMONT IF I DON’T HAVE A TRADITIONAL ADDRESS?
questions.a: Yes. If you do not have a traditional residential address, you can still register and vote in Vermont. You’ll need to provide a location description of where you typically stay or reside (such as a shelter, park, or intersection), and identify the town or city in Vermont where you consider yourself a resident.

questions.q: AM I REQUIRED TO SHOW ID TO REGISTER TO VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a: Yes, if you are registering for the first time by mail or online (https://vote.vermont.gov/public/dashboard), you must include a photocopy of an acceptable form of ID.

questions.q: WHAT TYPES OF ID CAN I USE TO REGISTER TO VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a:
If you register online (https://vote.vermont.gov/public/dashboard) or by mail for the first time in Vermont, you must include a photocopy of an acceptable ID with your application. Acceptable ID includes:

- A valid photo ID (like a Vermont driver’s license or a U.S. passport)
- A current utility bill
- A current bank statement
- Another government document that includes your name and residential address

In addition, you must provide either your Vermont driver’s license number, your Personal ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security Number on the application.

If you register in person at your town or city clerk’s office, you are not required to show ID. However, you still must provide your driver’s license number, your Personal ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security Number on the registration application.

questions.q: WHAT IF I DON’T HAVE THE REQUIRED ID WHEN I REGISTER IN VERMONT?
questions.a:
If you’re registering online or by mail and do not include a photocopy of an acceptable ID, your registration will not be complete and may be delayed or rejected. To avoid problems, either:

- Include one of the acceptable ID documents listed above, or
- Register in person at your local town clerk’s office. Photo ID is not required, but your identifying information will still be verified.

Voters can call or text 866-432-8683 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: What do I need to register to vote in Vermont?
questions.a:
Here is what you need to know to register in Vermont:

There are three methods of voter registration in Vermont: register in-person, register online (https://vote.vermont.gov/public/dashboard), or mail a printable application (https://outside.vermont.gov/dept/sos/Elections%20Division/voters/voterapplication.pdf) to your Town Clerk (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/town-clerks/).

questions.q: Can I register to vote using my college address in Vermont?
questions.a: Yes, if you consider your campus address your residence, you can register to vote there. If you move to a different dorm or off campus, be sure to update your voter registration with your new address so you vote in the correct district.

questions.q: What’s the deadline to register to vote in Vermont?
questions.a: Vermont does not have a voter registration deadline. You can register to vote at any time, even on Election Day. However, if you register online, it’s recommended to do so by the Friday before Election Day to ensure your name appears on the voter rolls on Election Day.

questions.q: What form of ID do I need to vote in Vermont?
questions.a: Voters in Vermont are not required to show identification to vote. However, first-time voters who registered by mail may be asked to present a form of ID at the polls, such as a driver’s license, passport, student ID from a state-supported college, or other accepted types.

questions.q: I’m originally from another state, can I still vote in my home state while studying in Vermont?
questions.a: Yes, you can vote in your home state using an absentee ballot, but you'll need to follow your home state's rules and deadlines. You can find the rules for your state on VOTE411 or by contacting your state’s election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm?_ga=2.80770708.201004602.1748545947-889989650.1701105430).

questions.q: Does registering to vote affect my financial aid, parents’ taxes, and/or tuition in Vermont?
questions.a: Registering to vote in your college community will not affect your Federal Financial Aid, status as a dependent on your parents’ taxes, or tuition status.

questions.q: DO I NEED TO SHOW ID WHEN I VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a: Most Vermont voters do not need to show ID when voting. However, if you are a first-time voter who registered by mail or online, you must show identification the first time you vote.

questions.q: WHAT TYPES OF ID CAN I USE TO VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a:
If you’re a first-time voter who registered by mail or online and did not provide verification when you registered, you can show any one of the following forms of identification at the polls:

- A valid photo ID (like a driver’s license or passport)
- A current utility bill
- A current bank statement
- A government document that includes your name and residential address

These documents can be physical copies or originals, as long as they clearly show your name and address.

questions.q: WHAT IF I DON’T HAVE AN ACCEPTABLE ID WHEN I GO TO VOTE IN VERMONT?
questions.a:
If you’re a first-time voter who registered by mail or online and did not provide verification when you registered, and you don’t have acceptable ID when you go to vote, you can still vote, but you may be asked to use a provisional ballot. Election officials will verify your eligibility before your vote is counted.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: Ballot Notice and Cure Process
questions.a:
The deadline to cure (correct) your absentee/mail ballot is 7 p.m. on Election Day. If your ballot is found incomplete or incorrect, the registrar will attempt to notify you of the error and how you can correct the issue. We recommend that you track the status of your ballot using your state’s online tool (http://vote.vermont.gov/) before Election Day to make sure it has been received and accepted.

If you voted a provisional ballot, election officials will do the research to determine if you are an eligible voter after the close of the polls. Questioned ballots are either counted or rejected 2 days after the election.

questions.q: Campaign Finance Information
questions.a:
For information on federal campaign contributions, please visit Open Secrets (http://www.opensecrets.org).

For information on state campaign contributions, please visit your state's resource. (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/campaign-finance/)

questions.q: Candidate and Ballot Measure Information
questions.a: Information on local, state and federal candidates and ballot measures may be available here (https://www.vote411.org/ballot#.UFoDEFHh-Sp). (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/election-info-resources/candidates/)

questions.q: Drop Boxes
questions.a: You can only use the dropbox of the city or town you vote from. A spreadsheet listing each town, whether it has a dropbox, and dropbox locations is downloadable at the Secretary of State site (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/). You can also drop off your ballot at your assigned polling location on election day.

questions.q: Early Voting
questions.a:
Early voting for the November 3, 2026 General Election begins on September 19th and ends November 2nd.

Early Voting Starts: 45 days before Election Day
Early Voting Ends: The day before Election Day

Note: Vermont conducts elections primarily by mail.

Early voting is also available with no excuse required. You may vote at your town clerk's office (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/town-clerks/) in person during the hours the office is open to the public, within 45 days before a primary or general election or 20 days before a municipal election. Due to the pandemic, Some Vermont town offices are closed to the public or have limited hours to protect health and safety, and most have a secure ballot drop box available whether or not the office is open. Please contact your town clerk. (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/town-clerks/)

questions.q: Election Dates
questions.a:
The next election dates can be found here https://www.vote411.org/vermont.

Contact your local Board of Elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: Election Day Voting Hours
questions.a:
All polls are open from between 5am and 10am and close at 7pm.

For local polling place hours, please visit the Vermont Voter Portal or call your local town clerk. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

questions.q: Official Election Results
questions.a:
Official results are never available on Election Day. Election officials are working around the clock to count an unprecedented number of ballots, and it’s essential that they take the time to make sure every vote is counted.

Official election results will be uploaded on Vermont’s Secretary of State website (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/election-info-resources/) as they become available.

  Official Results  (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/election-info-resources/)

questions.q: Overseas and Military Voters
questions.a:
You are a Military or Overseas voter if you are in uniformed services, living overseas OR a spouse or dependent of a uniformed services voter. To get registered and vote, you can utilize Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/about-contact)

If you have additional questions about elections and voting overseas you can use our state specific elections official directory or contact the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/about-contact)

questions.q: Poll Worker Information
questions.a:
You can make sure we have safe, fair, and efficient elections for all. Become a poll worker toda (https://powerthepolls.org/lwv )y!

In order to be a poll worker in Vermont, you must:

- Be registered to vote in Vermont
- Be entitled to compensation
- Be at least 18 years of age
- Political affiliation considered
- Be a resident of the voting district
- Complete required training
- Students who are 16 and 17 years old may be appointed as assistant elections officers

To sign up, contact your local board of elections (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Polling Place Locations
questions.a:
You can find your polling place by utilizing your state resource. (https://vote.vermont.gov/public/dashboard)

If you have further questions on your polling place location, please contact your county clerk. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

questions.q: Primary Election Process
questions.a:
Vermont is an “open primary” state. You can choose the party’s ballot you wish to vote. This decision does not register you with that party and it is a private decision.

In a primary election if candidates tie there will be a primary runoff election scheduled for a few weeks after the primary election date. The runoff election will have the top two candidates with the most votes to ensure that one of them receives the majority of the voters.

If you have any questions about your state’s primary election, please contact your local election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: Provisional Voting
questions.a:
A provisional ballot is only used if a person trying to vote at the polling place is not on the checklist and cannot affirm they registered to vote by the deadline.

Provisional ballots are counted 2 days after the election.

questions.q: Provisions for Voters with Disabilities
questions.a:
Voters with disabilities are able to vote, at their polling locations, using accessible voting technology. Voters will access a tablet-based system that marks your selection onto the same paper ballot used by all voters at the polls. This system also contains an online-based ballot marking system that allows voters with disabilities to vote privately and independently from home during the early voting period.

If you need help with voting, you can:

- Contact your Town Clerk to ask for accomodations
- Bring a person of your choice with you into the voting booth (not your employer or union representative)
- Ask an election official for help with marking your ballot
- Ask an election official to bring a ballot to your car
- Bring a magnifying glass or other devices to help you use the ballot
- Bring a list of candidates into the voting book with you
- Ask for another ballot (maximum of 3) if you make a mistake
- Use the Omniballot tablet accessible voting system at the polls.

For more information contact your Secretary of State. (https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/accessible-voting/)

questions.q: Time Off To Vote
questions.a: Time off to vote is subject to the employer, there is no requirement for employers to grant time off to vote for employees.

questions.q: Voter Registration Deadlines
questions.a:
The voter registration deadline for the Tuesday, November 3, 2026 General Election is November 3, 2026.

Online registration deadline: Election Day

Register by mail deadline: Received by Election Day

In-person registration deadline: Election Day

Not registered? Use our registration tool (https://www.vote411.org/register#.UFdk4FHh-So) to fill out your application!

questions.q: Voting Machines
questions.a:
The voting systems used in Vermont are optical scan, paper ballots and the Omniballot tablet system.

Optical Scan: With this system, you will receive a card or sheet of paper, which you take over to a private table or booth. The names of the various candidates and ballot measures are printed on the card. With a special pen or pencil located at the table or booth, you fill in the box or circle or the space between two arrows. When you are finished filling out the card, you may bring the card over to a ballot box, where poll workers will show you how to put the card in the box. Or in some places, you may feed the completed card or paper into a computer where the scanner ensures that your card was properly completed so that your vote will be counted.

Paper Ballots: Paper ballots are one of the oldest ways of voting in America. They are still used in a few places on Election Day. When you come to the polling place, you will get a paper ballot from the poll worker. You take it to the voting booth and use a pen or pencil to mark a box next to your candidate and issue choices. You then drop the marked ballot into a sealed ballot box.

Omniballot Tablet Accessible Voting System: In-person. Voters with disabilities may vote independently at their polling locations using accessible voting technology. Voters will access the tablet-based system that marks your selection onto the same paper ballot used by all voters at the polls.

Online: This system also contains an online-based ballot marking system that allows voters with disabilities to vote privately and independently from home through the VT Portal on the voter’s personal computer during the early voting period.
